title: Upper Primary 1
cefr: A1–A2: A1 consolidation toward A2 communication
entryExpectations: Broad A1 familiarity: exchange basic personal information; follow simple classroom instructions; recognise familiar everyday words; read and write short simple sentences with support. Use the existing welcome lesson as an entry diagnostic. Revisit gaps in question forms, sound–spelling links, everyday verbs and numbers before increasing task demands. A1 entry to A2-oriented outcomes is a planning target, not a guarantee from age or course completion. Pacing: Unit 1 has nine core 45-minute lessons plus conditional support/extension; later units remain provisional sketches. Adjust after entry evidence, classroom piloting and timetable decisions.

sources.title: Council of Europe (2020), CEFR Companion Volume
Council of Europe (2018), Young learner descriptor collation, ages 7–10
Council of Europe (2018), Young learner descriptor collation, ages 11–15

alignmentNote: Original WKE course objectives aligned to the cited CEFR scales and age-adapted using the young-learner collections. The twelve themes and grammar order are the school's curriculum choices; CEFR does not prescribe this grammar syllabus. Printed page numbers refer to the 2020 Companion Volume.

L.summary: Follow clear, slow speech about familiar needs.

R.summary: Read brief texts with familiar everyday vocabulary.

RO.summary: Locate predictable information in everyday written material.

RI.summary: Find key information in simple factual texts.

D.summary: Describe familiar people, places, routines and events.

P.summary: Give a prepared talk with supported follow-up.

W.summary: Connect short sentences on familiar topics.

CW.summary: Write simple descriptions and short event accounts.

I.summary: Exchange everyday facts and straightforward directions.

S.summary: Handle predictable purchases, quantities and prices.

G.summary: Participate in practical tasks with supportive partners.

Q.summary: Request repetition or explanation when necessary.

M.summary: Pass on relevant details from short sources.

T.scale: Expressing a personal response to creative texts (including literature)
T.summary: Respond simply to characters, feelings and events.

C.summary: Contribute to shared tasks with appropriate support.

CC.summary: Join ideas with basic linking expressions.

courseObjectives.statement: Identify the purpose and useful details in short spoken messages about the twelve course themes.
courseObjectives.learnerStatement: I can listen for the information I need.
courseObjectives.successCriteria: After a short, clear recording, identify its purpose and at least 3 useful details. Record repetitions, visuals and other support used.

courseObjectives.statement: Use short profiles, timetables, maps, labels and stories to find information for a classroom task.
courseObjectives.learnerStatement: I can read a short text and use its information.
courseObjectives.successCriteria: Locate 4 of 5 requested details in a familiar text type and use at least 2 to complete the task; rereading is allowed.

courseObjectives.statement: Sustain a brief peer exchange about a familiar topic, asking relevant questions and clarifying information.
courseObjectives.learnerStatement: I can ask, answer and check that I understand.
courseObjectives.successCriteria: Complete 4 relevant question-answer exchanges, contribute in both roles, and request repetition or clarification when needed.

courseObjectives.statement: Describe familiar people, routines, homes, schools and places, including relevant comparisons.
courseObjectives.learnerStatement: I can describe my world and compare things.
courseObjectives.successCriteria: Give 5–6 understandable statements with 3 relevant details and an appropriate comparison when the task calls for one; keyword cues are allowed.

courseObjectives.statement: Recount an event or construct a simple story with an understandable order of events.
courseObjectives.learnerStatement: I can tell what happened in order.
courseObjectives.successCriteria: Communicate at least 4 ordered events, use past-time language and 3 suitable connectors, and make the ending understandable.

courseObjectives.statement: Produce and revise a short description, message, advice note or story for a familiar reader.
courseObjectives.learnerStatement: I can write a short message that someone can understand.
courseObjectives.successCriteria: Produce 6–8 relevant linked sentences, then improve meaning and at least 2 language or presentation features using a checklist.

courseObjectives.statement: Help a partner complete a practical task by sharing source information, suggesting an action and responding.
courseObjectives.learnerStatement: I can share useful information and help my group decide.
courseObjectives.successCriteria: Pass on 3 accurate details from a short source, make one relevant suggestion, respond to a partner, and record any help with formulation.

courseObjectives.statement: Present a familiar discovery using selected facts, descriptions and simple explanations, then answer questions.
courseObjectives.learnerStatement: I can share a discovery and answer questions about it.
courseObjectives.successCriteria: Give a prepared 1–2-minute talk using visuals or keywords, communicate 4 sourced facts and one explanation, and answer 2 straightforward questions with repetition/support recorded.

units.title: Who Am I?
units.languageFocus: Present simple statements and questions; be/greetings; like/enjoy; be good at; always, usually, often, sometimes, never.
units.example: I usually draw after school. I am good at solving puzzles.
units.outcome: Introduce yourself, describe interests and strengths, and exchange information about familiar routines.
units.assessmentTask: Help a new classmate find a shared activity through an individual learner profile and interview; collect fresh listening and reading evidence separately, plus revised writing and individual speaking.
units.support: Picture profiles, hobby/strength cards, a frequency line and question frames; fade full sentence models before the checkpoint. Fictional profiles are acceptable.
units.extension: Add a relevant reason with because and one unscripted follow-up question; compare two routines without making this a core requirement.

objectives.statement: Find personal details, interests and routine information in short spoken or written learner profiles.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can understand a short profile.
objectives.successCriteria: Identify 4 of 5 details across a new short profile, including an interest and a frequency detail; record replay or picture support.

objectives.statement: Exchange information about interests, strengths and routines with a partner.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can ask about interests and say what I often do.
objectives.successCriteria: Ask and answer 4 relevant questions; communicate 2 interests/strengths and use 2 frequency expressions appropriately. Clarify if needed.

objectives.statement: Create a short learner profile describing strengths, interests and weekly routines.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can tell others about myself and my routines.
objectives.successCriteria: Produce 6–8 understandable linked sentences covering strengths, interests and routines, including 3 frequency expressions; share a brief oral version from keywords.

lessons.title: L2 Vocabulary — My interests and strengths
lessons.task:
CORE L2 — vocabulary. 5m Retrieve: Hide models; retrieve welcome greetings and name/age. Exchange information; then check one model.
8m Model: Mime/draw the six activities; model like + activity-ing and good at as chunks. Match meaning, say each chunk and choose an interest.
10m Guide: Model two examples and sound–spelling links. Sort activity cards and pair a chunk with an example.
12m Apply: Offer personal/fictional choices and a short partner task. Choose an interest and strength; explain two useful choices.
7m Check: Use seven meaning/picture cues without the printed words. Retrieve chunks, then make two meaningful statements.
3m Reflect: Name the next listening purpose and support route. Choose one chunk to retrieve next lesson.

lessons.title: SUPPORT S1 — Hobby meanings and sound–spelling
lessons.task:
SUPPORT S1 — vocabulary. 3m Retrieve: Identify the particular missing chunks. Attempt four cues.
5m Model: Connect meaning, spoken chunk and written form. Mime, listen and point.
7m Guide: Build and sort selected chunk cards. Say/read the chunks in supported examples.
7m Apply: Change the cue and remove the full model. Retrieve the four selected chunks and use two.
3m Recheck: Record what help remains. Choose a cue tool for L3.
Route: Use when L2 shows persistent meaning/form confusion, rather than one slip. For example, fewer than four chunks are accessible even after normal picture cues. This is a local routing cue, not a CEFR cut-score.

lessons.title: L3 Listening — Find useful profile details
lessons.task:
CORE L3 — listening. 5m Retrieve: Give changed meaning cues for three L2 chunks. Retrieve, then check meanings.
8m Model: Read listenModel naturally and clearly; model gist first, then one detail. Explain frequency meanings with everyday examples. Identify the purpose: meeting a classmate.
10m Guide: Read the same model again; use a five-box fact grid and model a repetition request. Find five details and check with the teacher.
12m Apply: Read listenCheck; provide no transcript. Allow a second clear reading and record it. Answer five checks by pointing/brief notes and suggest a shared activity.
7m Check: Collect individual responses and ask which fact supports the suggestion. Use a heard detail to justify the choice.
3m Reflect: After the check, allow transcript review and clarify an error. Name a useful listening strategy.

lessons.title: L4 Grammar — How often do you do it?
lessons.task:
CORE L4 — grammar. 5m Retrieve: Recall one heard profile detail without a transcript. Say the activity/frequency and check it.
8m Model: Contrast frequency meanings and place the adverb before an action verb; model do questions. Notice meaning and the familiar routine pattern.
10m Guide: Use the five meaning items and the two model question/answer strips in the teacher pack. Choose meanings, build statements and ask a question.
12m Apply: Give a real or fictional routine grid; fade full frames to keywords. Create three statements using two frequencies, then ask a partner.
7m Check: Use the fresh five meaning checks, plus individual statements/question. Interpret and communicate without copying a full model.
3m Reflect: Identify a specific support need. Choose S2 if the pattern remains inaccessible.

lessons.title: SUPPORT S2 — Routine questions and frequency meaning
lessons.task:
SUPPORT S2 — grammar. 3m Retrieve: Locate the particular confusion. Choose meaning or attempt a question.
5m Model: Contrast two meanings with a concrete routine; rebuild one do question. Explain by pointing/acting.
7m Guide: Use movable word strips, then remove a strip. Build and ask meaningful questions.
7m Apply: Change the routine and reduce cues. Make two statements and ask a new question.
3m Recheck: Check three meaning items and record remaining support. Select a useful cue for the core path.
Route: Use when meaning is confused (for example never/often) or learners cannot build an understandable routine question after ordinary frames and feedback.

lessons.title: L5 Reading — Read a profile and choose an activity
lessons.task:
CORE L5 — reading. 5m Retrieve: Retrieve two frequency meanings and a hobby from earlier lessons. Use them in a short routine statement.
8m Model: Show readPractice; think aloud about locating one fact and checking a pronoun/reference. Read for the purpose of finding a shared activity.
10m Guide: Use the linked Linh reading activity or its paper version. Find five details; point to the supporting words.
12m Apply: Provide readCheck, not the final checkpoint text. Find five details independently with rereading and choose a shared activity.
7m Check: Ask for two facts that support the activity choice; accept brief oral/pointed evidence. Show the facts in the text.
3m Reflect: Give one locating/checking tip after the check. Correct one response and explain the useful strategy.

lessons.title: L6 Speaking — Interview, listen and clarify
lessons.task:
CORE L6 — speaking. 5m Retrieve: Retrieve two questions from earlier oral practice without full models. Ask and answer a familiar question.
8m Model: Demonstrate the four-question interview, both roles and one clarification/confirmation. Notice turn-taking and checking a detail.
10m Guide: Provide role cards and one rehearsal with full frames. Interview with support and note keywords, not a full script.
12m Apply: Change partners or fictional cards; reduce to keyword prompts. Take both roles and check one genuinely unclear or deliberately missed detail.
7m Check: Observe individual turns and use a new question/detail. Finish observations in the next lesson if class size requires it. Complete four exchanges and confirm/clarify a detail.
3m Reflect: Give one meaningful communication improvement. Retry one response and retain useful notes for writing.

lessons.title: L7 Writing — Create and improve my learner profile
lessons.task:
CORE L7 — writing. 5m Retrieve: Retrieve one routine and one strength chunk. Orally rehearse without copying the model.
8m Model: Use the short profile model and think aloud about audience and sentence order. Identify interest, strength and three frequency expressions.
10m Guide: Use the profile planner, then replace full frames with keywords where possible. Plan own or fictional details and rehearse with a partner.
12m Apply: Remove the complete model while keeping agreed word/access tools. Write an individual 6–8-sentence profile.
7m Check: Use the revision checklist and give focused feedback. Improve two features and keep the first draft.
3m Reflect: Record actual help and one next step. Select one useful change for the final profile.

lessons.title: L8 Review — Retrieve, apply and improve
lessons.task:
CORE L8 — review. 5m Retrieve: Use welcome prompts plus three changed meaning cues; show models only after attempts. Retrieve and self-check.
8m Model: Address one shared misconception with a contrasting example. Explain its meaning rather than copy it.
10m Guide: Run three short stations: vocabulary retrieval, frequency/meaning choice, interview repair. Attempt each, receive feedback and try a changed example.
12m Apply: Use review profile Jo and new questions, keeping final texts unseen. Find useful facts and suggest a shared activity in a fresh exchange.
7m Check: Recheck each learner’s priority gap using a different cue/task. Revise one earlier oral/written response.
3m Reflect: Prepare learners for the final conditions and arrange targeted follow-up. Name one strength and a next step.

lessons.title: L9 Checkpoint — My learner profile and Unit 2 bridge
lessons.task:
CORE L9 — checkpoint. 4m Orient: Greet and exchange names/ages/feelings; explain support and keep final sources unseen. Prepare a fact grid and keyword card.
6m Listen: Read finalListen clearly twice; record any further replay. Answer five short/listen-and-point checks.
7m Read: Provide finalRead; permit rereading. Answer five checks and choose a shared activity with two text facts.
10m Write: Collect the L7 draft and allow an individual final revision. Submit a 6–8-sentence profile with two noted improvements.
12m Speak: Observe each learner’s brief profile and four-exchange interview; use observation stations or continue next lesson for unobserved learners. Share from keywords, take both roles and check a detail.
6m Bridge: Reflect on one strength/next step; use the school-routine bridge card. Read a simple school-day card and say one familiar routine; note time/subject gaps for Unit 2.

lessons.title: OPTIONAL E1 — A class interests gallery
lessons.task:
EXTENSION E1 — integration. 4m Retrieve: Recall useful invitation/profile language. Prepare a keyword response.
6m Plan: Set a small gallery purpose and privacy choices. Choose two profile details and a display format.
12m Apply: Use a new partner/audience with familiar language. Read a profile, invite a shared activity and ask/answer a follow-up.
5m Feedback: Observe individual communication and give one suggestion. Improve a short message or response.
3m Reflect: Record an optional stretch achievement without replacing core evidence. Choose one future use of the language.
Route: Offer after the core outcome is accessible and learners want a wider audience. Provide an equivalent private/fictional display option; sharing personal work is a choice.

units.guideStatus: Exemplar: 9 core lessons, 2 conditional support workshops and 1 optional extension; classroom pacing to be piloted.

focusObjectives.statement: Retrieve and use familiar interest and strength chunks for a learner profile.
focusObjectives.learnerStatement: I can remember useful words for my interests and strengths.
focusObjectives.successCriteria: Retrieve 6 of 7 selected hobby/strength chunks from meaning or picture cues, then use 2 in relevant personal or fictional statements; record cue support.

focusObjectives.statement: Find useful identity, interest, strength and frequency information in a short spoken profile.
focusObjectives.learnerStatement: I can listen to a profile and find useful details.
focusObjectives.successCriteria: Identify 4 of 5 details in a fresh spoken profile, including an interest and frequency detail; use a fact to select a suitable shared activity. Record replays and visuals.

focusObjectives.statement: Interpret and use present-simple routine statements, frequency expressions and do questions.
focusObjectives.learnerStatement: I can say how often I do things and ask about routines.
focusObjectives.successCriteria: Interpret 4 of 5 meaning contrasts; communicate 3 relevant routine statements with 2 frequency expressions and ask one understandable do question. Record model use.

focusObjectives.statement: Use information from a short written learner profile to make a relevant choice.
focusObjectives.learnerStatement: I can read a profile and choose an activity that fits.
focusObjectives.successCriteria: Find 4 of 5 requested details in a fresh written profile; support a suitable activity choice with 2 text facts. Rereading is allowed; record glossary support.

focusObjectives.statement: Interview a peer about interests, strengths and routines, taking both roles and checking meaning.
focusObjectives.learnerStatement: I can ask, answer and check information with a partner.
focusObjectives.successCriteria: Complete 4 relevant question-answer exchanges in both roles, communicate 2 interests/strengths and 2 frequency expressions, and check or clarify a detail when needed.

focusObjectives.statement: Plan, write and revise an individual learner profile for a classmate.
focusObjectives.learnerStatement: I can write a useful profile and improve it for my reader.
focusObjectives.successCriteria: Write 6–8 linked sentences including an interest, a strength and 3 frequency expressions; improve 2 features after feedback. Record frames, word bank or scribing used.

units.nextUnitBridge: Use a school-day card: I read stories at school. Art: 9:00; Reading: 10:00. Ask learners to locate Reading at ten and say a familiar school routine. Record subject/clock gaps for U2 L1; teach a missing phrase briefly. Do not require earlier/later/than yet.

libraryResources.title: UP1 Unit 1 — Interests, strengths and routines
libraryResources.purpose: Editable 12-entry language source; select the first seven in L2 and frequency words in L4.

libraryResources.title: UP1 Unit 1 — Meaning-to-chunk retrieval cards
libraryResources.purpose: 12 text-only retrieval cards, definition on front and word/example on back; supported practice.

libraryResources.title: UP1 Unit 1 — Read Linh’s learner profile
libraryResources.purpose: Linh practice passage and five validated questions; follow with a source-based activity choice.

units.title: School Life Around the World
units.themeFocus: Subjects, schedules and comparisons between individual schools
units.languageFocus: School subjects and clock times; present simple; comparative adjectives/adverbs; earlier/later/longer than; our/their and ours/theirs.
units.example: Our school starts earlier than theirs.
units.outcome: Read school-day information, compare two schools and share a clear description of your own school day.
units.assessmentTask: Partner-school exchange: interpret two timetables, discuss comparisons and write a short school-day message.
units.support: Colour-coded timetables, clock visuals, comparison strips and a short message model. Describe particular schools rather than making claims about all children in a country.
units.extension: Explain a preference with because and ask one question about the partner school.

objectives.statement: Retrieve subjects, times and routine details from two short school profiles and timetables.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can read and compare school-day information.
objectives.successCriteria: Locate 4 of 5 requested subject/time facts and match each to the correct school; rereading and clock visuals are allowed.

objectives.statement: Compare two school days using information from their timetables.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can say how two school days are different.
objectives.successCriteria: Give 3 accurate comparisons about times, subjects or length, using than and making clear whose school each statement describes.

objectives.statement: Write a short message introducing a school day to a partner class.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can write about our school day for another class.
objectives.successCriteria: Write 6–8 linked sentences with 3 timetable facts, 2 comparisons and a relevant question; revise one unclear detail after feedback.

lessons.title: Read two school days
lessons.task: Begin with a short greeting/name/age/feeling exchange from Unit 1. Read two school profiles and timetables; locate subjects, start times and breaks. Listen to one school-day description and match it to the correct timetable. Check facts using clocks and highlighting, then ask a partner to confirm a missing detail.

lessons.title: Compare our timetables
lessons.task: Model earlier/later/longer than from the same timetables, then practise our/their and ours/theirs with clear referents. Partners hold different timetables, exchange missing information, and agree on three true comparisons. Revisit present-simple routines and frequency expressions from Unit 1.

lessons.title: A message to a partner school
lessons.task: Pairs decide which school-day facts would interest a partner class, each contributing one suggestion. Individually write a 6–8-sentence message with timetable facts, comparisons and a question. Peer-check factual accuracy and who each pronoun refers to; revise before sharing.

lessons.title: School-life exchange: unit checkpoint
lessons.task: Provide two fresh, accessible school timetables. Check five facts, hear each learner give three comparisons in a short partner exchange, and collect an individual school-day message. Assess the three criteria separately and record support; do not assess national stereotypes or cultural knowledge.

units.title: Home Sweet Home
units.languageFocus: There is/are and place prepositions; have to/don't have to for responsibilities; present-simple questions.
units.example: I have to tidy my room.
units.outcome: Describe a home or imaginary room and explain a fair set of household responsibilities.
units.assessmentTask: Home tour and chore agreement: interpret a floor plan, agree on responsibilities and present a simple home plan.
units.support: Labelled floor plans, movable furniture icons and chore cards; use an imaginary home so no learner needs to reveal home circumstances.
units.extension: Compare two rooms and explain why one arrangement works better.

objectives.statement: Locate rooms, furniture and responsibilities in a simple home plan and chore chart.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can understand a home plan and chore chart.
objectives.successCriteria: Identify 4 of 5 room/furniture/chore details and correctly locate 2 items using the plan.

objectives.statement: Agree on household responsibilities in a short partner exchange.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can say what I have to do and ask about chores.
objectives.successCriteria: Complete 4 exchanges and agree on 3 responsibilities using have to; distinguish something unnecessary with don't have to.

objectives.statement: Present a simple home plan with furniture locations and household responsibilities.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can give a short home tour and explain our chores.
objectives.successCriteria: Communicate 3 accurate locations and 3 responsibilities in 6–8 linked sentences; use a labelled plan and keywords rather than a full oral script.

lessons.title: Explore homes and rooms
lessons.task: Read a simple floor plan and chore chart, matching rooms, furniture and responsibilities. Revisit Unit 1 routines with two frequency statements. Use there is/are and prepositions to locate furniture, then check understanding against a different room plan.

lessons.title: Who does which chores?
lessons.task: Model have to and don't have to through contrasting chore cards; show that not necessary is different from not allowed. Partners ask about chores and agree on three responsibilities for fictional housemates. Revisit how often questions and frequency expressions.

lessons.title: Design a fair home plan
lessons.task: Pairs arrange an imaginary room and a fair chore chart, exchanging suggestions and comparing two possible layouts using Unit 2 language. Each learner prepares their own 6–8-sentence home description with three locations and responsibilities, then gives a brief tour from a diagram.

lessons.title: Home tour and chores: unit checkpoint
lessons.task: Use a fresh floor plan/chore chart for five checks. Observe a four-exchange chore agreement and collect each learner's home description plus short tour. Assess information, responsibility meanings and understandable description separately; record support and plan feedback/recheck.

units.title: Healthy Living
units.languageFocus: Should/shouldn't for advice; present-simple habits and frequency; because for a simple reason.
units.example: You should exercise and eat vegetables.
units.outcome: Understand familiar wellbeing information, offer kind everyday advice and plan realistic habits.
units.assessmentTask: Wellbeing buddy plan: interpret a fictional weekly log, discuss advice and write a realistic habit plan.
units.support: Picture logs, choice cards and advice frames. Focus on wellbeing and varied habits, not body size, food shame, diagnosis or treatment.
units.extension: Compare two practical choices and explain which suits the fictional learner's routine.

objectives.statement: Identify habits and practical wellbeing information in a short weekly log or recording.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can understand information about everyday habits.
objectives.successCriteria: Identify 4 of 5 details about food, movement, sleep or water in a fictional log; record any replay or visual support.

objectives.statement: Offer and respond to simple, kind advice about everyday wellbeing habits.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can give useful advice and explain a simple reason.
objectives.successCriteria: Offer 3 relevant should/shouldn't suggestions, give a simple reason for 2, and respond to a partner's suggestion without judging their body or circumstances.

objectives.statement: Write a realistic weekly wellbeing plan linked to a learner's routine.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can plan habits that help me feel well.
objectives.successCriteria: Write 6 linked sentences covering 3 realistic habits, their frequency and one reason; distinguish a chosen habit from a required responsibility.

lessons.title: Discover everyday wellbeing
lessons.task: Retrieve frequency expressions from Unit 1. Read/listen to fictional weekly logs and identify routines involving varied food, movement, sleep and water. Match information to pictures and answer five detail questions; keep discussion practical and non-judgemental.

lessons.title: Give kind, practical advice
lessons.task: Model should/shouldn't with familiar habit cards and because for a brief reason. In pairs, offer three relevant suggestions to a fictional learner and respond to advice. Compare advice with Unit 3 have to responsibilities; practise asking for repetition or a clearer example.

lessons.title: Make a weekly wellbeing plan
lessons.task: Choose three manageable habits for a fictional or personal weekly plan. Partners share log details and discuss realistic frequencies, then each learner writes six linked sentences. Peer-check whether the advice fits the routine and revise one unrealistic or unclear suggestion.

lessons.title: Wellbeing buddy plan: unit checkpoint
lessons.task: Use a new fictional habit log for five checks, hear three advice suggestions with reasons, and collect an individual weekly plan. Score understanding, communication and advice meanings separately. Nutrition knowledge, appearance and medical decision-making are not language assessment criteria.

units.title: Our Amazing Planet
units.languageFocus: Superlatives with the; comparative review; descriptive adjectives; simple because explanations.
units.example: The Pacific is the largest ocean.
units.outcome: Use simple source information to describe and compare places and explain a habitat feature.
units.assessmentTask: Planet discovery gallery: read fact cards, compare places and explain a labelled habitat factfile.
units.support: Verified, teacher-selected short fact cards, maps, pictures and a comparison chart; teach unfamiliar science words in context.
units.extension: Add a second source fact and explain a simple cause using because without requiring a technical scientific explanation.

objectives.statement: Retrieve landscape and habitat facts from short labelled maps and fact cards.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can find facts about places and habitats.
objectives.successCriteria: Find 4 of 5 requested facts and match 2 places or animals to the appropriate habitat; distinguish source facts from guesses.

objectives.statement: Describe and compare familiar landscapes using supported geographical facts.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can compare amazing places.
objectives.successCriteria: Communicate 3 source-consistent facts, including 2 appropriate superlatives and one comparison; make the comparison group clear.

objectives.statement: Create and explain a short habitat factfile with labelled features.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can explain what makes a habitat special.
objectives.successCriteria: Use a map/picture and 6 linked sentences to give location, 3 habitat facts and a simple because explanation; answer one familiar question with support recorded.

lessons.title: Explore landscapes and habitats
lessons.task: Locate landscapes on a map and read short teacher-verified habitat fact cards. Revisit home/location descriptions from Unit 3. Sort source facts from guesses, match animals to habitats, and complete five information checks using a picture glossary where needed.

lessons.title: Compare Earth's amazing places
lessons.task: Retrieve Unit 2 comparative language, then model the largest/highest/longest and the comparison group. Partners use different fact cards to give three accurate comparisons/superlatives and confirm the facts in a shared chart. Do not reward unsupported superlative claims.

lessons.title: Create a habitat factfile
lessons.task: Learners select a familiar habitat from supplied sources, label a map/picture and write six linked sentences. Exchange three useful source details with a partner, explain one habitat feature with because, and rehearse a brief factfile explanation from keywords.

lessons.title: Planet discovery gallery: unit checkpoint
lessons.task: Provide a fresh accessible map/fact card for comprehension. Hear three supported comparisons/superlatives, collect the factfile and ask one straightforward follow-up question. Record source accuracy and language performance separately; allow visuals and note formulation help.

units.title: The Mystery of the Past
units.languageFocus: Past simple regular/irregular verbs; was/were; did questions and negatives; first/next/then/finally.
units.example: We found a clue. Then we asked the caretaker what happened.
units.outcome: Understand a simple past-event account, ask about what happened and produce an ordered recount.
units.assessmentTask: Solve a classroom mystery: interpret clues, interview a fictional witness and recount the event sequence.
units.support: Picture timeline, short clue cards, a small regular/irregular verb bank and did-question frames; no graphic or frightening content.
units.extension: Offer a second possible explanation using a supplied clue, without requiring past perfect or complex inference.

objectives.statement: Identify people, places, times and event order in a short past-event account.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can understand the clues and order what happened.
objectives.successCriteria: Answer 4 of 5 who/where/when/event questions and order 4 events from a fresh short account; record replay or picture support.

objectives.statement: Ask and answer simple questions about a past event using clue information.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can ask what happened and share a clue.
objectives.successCriteria: Complete 4 relevant exchanges about who, where, when or what happened; use did/was/were questions and understandable past-time answers.

objectives.statement: Produce an ordered recount of a familiar or fictional past event.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can recount an event in the right order.
objectives.successCriteria: Communicate 4 events in 6–8 linked sentences, including a mix of regular/irregular past verbs and 3 sequence markers; meaning and event order stay clear despite minor errors.

lessons.title: Read the clues: what happened?
lessons.task: Retrieve present-simple routines from Unit 1 and contrast every day with yesterday. Read/listen to a short, non-threatening classroom mystery with picture clues. Identify who/where/when and place four events on a timeline; check against a fresh short account.

lessons.title: Build a past-event timeline
lessons.task: Model was/were, a small useful set of regular/irregular past verbs, and first/next/then/finally. Learners reconstruct four events from pictures, practise understandable regular -ed endings, and draft a 6–8-sentence recount. Revisit place descriptions from Unit 3 to say where events occurred.

lessons.title: Interview a witness and recount
lessons.task: Partners hold different fictional witness cards, ask did/was/were questions and exchange four useful facts, clarifying unclear clues. Each writes or records their own event recount from a timeline, checks it against the evidence, and improves an unclear past-time reference.

lessons.title: Solve the mystery: unit checkpoint
lessons.task: Give a fresh short clue account for comprehension and event ordering. Observe four past-event exchanges and collect an individual 6–8-sentence recount. Assess understanding, question-answer meaning and narrative order separately; note support and recheck misconceptions later.

units.title: Let's Go Shopping
units.languageFocus: How much does it cost?/How much are...?; I'd like/Can I have...?; some/any; countable/uncountable quantities; cheaper/the cheapest review.
units.example: How much does it cost? I'd like two notebooks, please.
units.outcome: Interpret simple price information and complete a polite shopping exchange with quantities and a budget.
units.assessmentTask: Class shop: read a price list, buy/sell two items and explain a small shopping plan.
units.support: Picture price lists, pretend money, quantity cards and role cues. Calculators are allowed; arithmetic and language are recorded separately.
units.extension: Compare two suitable purchases and explain a choice using cheaper/cheapest and because.

objectives.statement: Locate item, quantity and price details in a simple price list or receipt.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can read prices and quantities.
objectives.successCriteria: Find 4 of 5 item/quantity/price details, including a spoken price confirmation; use pretend currency and calculator support where needed.

objectives.statement: Complete a polite shopping exchange as buyer and seller.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can ask a price and buy what I need.
objectives.successCriteria: Complete at least 4 exchanges to request 2 items, ask/confirm prices and quantities, and close politely; clarify an unclear amount instead of guessing.

objectives.statement: Prepare and explain a simple shopping plan using a supplied budget and price list.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can choose items and explain my shopping plan.
objectives.successCriteria: List 3 items with quantities/prices and explain 2 choices in understandable sentences; keep a supplied budget with calculator support, scored separately from language.

lessons.title: Read prices and quantities
lessons.task: Retrieve welcome-lesson numbers 1–15, then extend price-reading as needed using a visible number chart. Read a picture price list and listen to short price confirmations. Match products, quantities, containers and prices; check five details without requiring mental arithmetic.

lessons.title: Ask, pay and clarify
lessons.task: Model polite buyer/seller exchanges, How much does it cost?, quantities and some/any. Pairs swap roles to request two items, confirm prices and clarify one unclear amount. Revisit Unit 2 comparisons and Unit 5 cheapest language when choosing between supplied options.

lessons.title: Plan a small class shop
lessons.task: Give a small pretend budget and fixed price list. Partners share item information and suggest choices, revisiting Unit 4 advice where useful. Each learner writes a three-item shopping plan and explains two choices with because; calculators support arithmetic while language is checked separately.

lessons.title: Class shop: unit checkpoint
lessons.task: Use a fresh price list for five checks. Observe each learner in buyer and seller roles and collect an individual shopping plan. Assess price/quantity communication, polite exchanges and reasons separately; do not treat arithmetic mistakes as automatic language failure.

units.title: My City, My Community
units.languageFocus: Where is...? / How can I get to...?; imperatives; go straight/turn left/right; next to/opposite/between; route sequence.
units.example: Go straight, turn left at the library, and the clinic is opposite the park.
units.outcome: Use a local map to locate services and give understandable directions to a destination.
units.assessmentTask: Community visitor guide: follow a route, give a partner directions and write a short visitor note.
units.support: Simple contrasting maps, route arrows, landmark pictures and direction strips; use fictional locations rather than personal addresses.
units.extension: Compare two routes with shorter/longer and explain a route choice.

objectives.statement: Interpret a simple community map and follow short directions to a service.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can use a map and follow directions.
objectives.successCriteria: Match 4 of 5 buildings/services to map information and reach the intended destination on a new short route; record repetition or arrow support.

objectives.statement: Ask for and give directions using a map, landmarks and ordered instructions.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can explain how to get somewhere.
objectives.successCriteria: Give 4–6 ordered steps that take a partner to the intended place, use 2 location/landmark phrases, and respond to a clarification question.

objectives.statement: Write a simple visitor guide explaining a service and how to reach it.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can write directions for a visitor.
objectives.successCriteria: Write a relevant service description and 4–6 route steps, with a clear starting point, landmarks and destination; revise after a partner follows the route.

lessons.title: Explore community services and maps
lessons.task: Retrieve Unit 3 place prepositions and Unit 7 service encounters. Match community buildings to services on a fictional map. Listen to short routes and locate destinations, checking starting points and landmarks rather than memorising a single route.

lessons.title: Ask for and give a route
lessons.task: Model ordered imperative directions with landmarks and Where is/How can I get to questions. Partners use contrasting maps to exchange missing routes, trace what they hear and ask for clarification when a turn is unclear. Revisit simple should advice for a visitor when useful.

lessons.title: Write a community visitor guide
lessons.task: Each learner chooses a useful service on the supplied map and writes a short description plus 4–6 route steps. A partner follows the written route and reports any unclear step. Share map details, revise the guide, and optionally compare two routes using earlier comparative language.

lessons.title: Guide a visitor: unit checkpoint
lessons.task: Provide an unfamiliar but simple map of familiar services. Check understanding of a short route, hear each learner guide a partner to a destination, and collect the revised visitor note. Assess reaching the destination and clarity of directions; record all repetition or formulation support.

units.title: Wonderful Inventions
units.themeFocus: Materials, uses and purposes of familiar inventions
units.languageFocus: We use a/an ... to + verb; It is for ...; material adjectives/nouns; is made of as a useful chunk, not a full passive-voice syllabus.
units.example: We use a thermometer to measure temperature.
units.outcome: Explain what familiar objects are made of and used for, then describe a simple invention for a classroom need.
units.assessmentTask: Young inventors expo: interpret object cards, describe uses and present a labelled classroom invention.
units.support: Safe object pictures, material samples/pictures, use-to frames and labelled diagrams; teach made of as a chunk and avoid hazardous construction tasks.
units.extension: Compare two designs, add a second use and explain which works better for a stated need.

objectives.statement: Match familiar invention descriptions to their materials, parts and uses.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can find out what an object is made of and used for.
objectives.successCriteria: Identify 4 of 5 material/use/part details from short object cards and correctly match 2 tools to a stated need.

objectives.statement: Describe the material and purpose of familiar objects in a short exchange.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can explain what we use an object to do.
objectives.successCriteria: Explain the material and purpose of 2 objects, using 2 understandable use-to statements and an accurate material description for each.

objectives.statement: Present a labelled invention idea that solves a familiar classroom problem.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can explain my invention and how it helps.
objectives.successCriteria: Label 3 parts/materials, identify the need, explain 2 uses with to + verb, and answer 2 simple questions using diagram/keyword support.

lessons.title: Match tools to everyday problems
lessons.task: Read short cards for safe, familiar inventions and match materials, parts and uses to pictures. Retrieve Unit 3 object locations and Unit 7 quantities with a simple materials list. Distinguish what an object does from what it is made of, then check five details on a new card.

lessons.title: Explain materials and purposes
lessons.task: Model We use ... to ... and made of as a short useful chunk. Partners hold different object cards and ask about material and purpose. Retrieve Unit 5 superlatives in a two-minute fact-card comparison, then make four clear material/purpose statements.

lessons.title: Design a classroom invention
lessons.task: Pairs suggest solutions to a familiar classroom need and agree on a safe imaginary design. Each learner labels three parts/materials and explains two uses from their own diagram. Use a simple supplied materials/quantity list, share relevant source facts, and rehearse two follow-up questions.

lessons.title: Young inventors expo: unit checkpoint
lessons.task: Use a fresh object card for five detail checks. Hear each learner explain two familiar objects, then present their labelled invention and answer two simple questions. Assess the need/use/material meanings and individual language performance; drawing or engineering polish is not a language score.

units.title: Stories That Inspire
units.themeFocus: Characters, problems, choices and narrative sequence
units.languageFocus: Past-simple retrieval; first/then/after that/finally; suddenly; and/but/because/so for simple links.
units.outcome: Understand a simple inspiring story, explain a response to a character and create a short coherent story.
units.assessmentTask: Story circle: interpret a new illustrated story, discuss a character's choice and share an original short story.
units.support: Illustrated story, event cards, story mountain, small past-verb bank and connector strip; no graphic violence or required personal disclosures.
units.extension: Add character speech or a different ending; past continuous is optional extension rather than a required new tense.

objectives.statement: Identify characters, the problem, key events and ending in a short illustrated story.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can understand who did what in a story.
objectives.successCriteria: Identify the character/problem/ending and order 4 key events from a fresh accessible story, with rereading allowed.

objectives.statement: Explain a simple personal response to a character's action using story evidence.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can say what I think about a character and why.
objectives.successCriteria: State a feeling or opinion about a character, support it with 2 story details, and respond to one partner question; a phrase bank is allowed.

objectives.statement: Create and share an understandable short story with a problem and resolution.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can create a story with a clear order and ending.
objectives.successCriteria: Write or tell 8–10 short linked sentences with 4 ordered events, a problem/resolution, past-time language and 3 suitable connectors; revise one confusing link.

lessons.title: Read an inspiring story
lessons.task: Retrieve Unit 6 past verbs and timeline language. Read/listen to a short illustrated story, identify character/problem/ending, and sequence four events. Discuss strengths from Unit 1 through what characters do rather than unsupported personality labels.

lessons.title: Link events and explain a character's choice
lessons.task: Use event cards to practise first/then/after that/finally and suddenly; compare and/but/because/so through meaning. Partners describe a character's choice, cite two story details and ask a simple follow-up. Reconstruct a short narrative with an understandable order.

lessons.title: Create, share and revise a story
lessons.task: Plan an original, age-appropriate story with a character, problem, four events and resolution. Write 8–10 short sentences using a small past-verb/connector bank. A partner listens or reads, asks about one unclear event and gives one useful response; revise before the story circle.

lessons.title: Story circle: unit checkpoint
lessons.task: Check comprehension and event order with a new short story. Hear an individual character response supported by two details, then collect/share the learner's revised original story. Score understanding, supported response and coherent story separately, recording any prompts or reference help.

units.title: Our Changing World
units.themeFocus: Local environmental care, responsibilities and practical action
units.languageFocus: Must/mustn't for obligation/prohibition; have to/don't have to review; should for advice; because for simple reasons.
units.outcome: Understand simple environmental messages, distinguish rules from advice and propose practical actions with reasons.
units.assessmentTask: Our eco-action plan: interpret notices, explain rules/advice and agree on a safe school or community action.
units.support: Picture notices, action-choice cards and contrasting rule/advice examples; discuss safe, supervised or hypothetical action rather than unsupervised river clean-up.
units.extension: Compare two actions and explain which better addresses a supplied local problem.

objectives.statement: Interpret simple environmental notices and identify the action they require or discourage.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can understand environmental notices.
objectives.successCriteria: Match 4 of 5 notices to the appropriate action and identify the intended rule or advice; explain one key sign in everyday words.

objectives.statement: Explain a simple environmental rule, prohibition and recommendation in a familiar situation.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can explain what we must, mustn't and should do.
objectives.successCriteria: Give 2 obligations, one prohibition and one suggestion that fit the situation; distinguish mustn't from don't have to through a concrete example.

objectives.statement: Collaborate on a practical environmental action plan and explain individual responsibilities.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can help make an action plan and explain my part.
objectives.successCriteria: Each learner contributes a suggestion and response, then records 3 suitable actions/responsibilities and 2 simple reasons; note any help with formulation.

lessons.title: Read the signs: our environment
lessons.task: Retrieve Unit 5 habitat facts and read short environmental notices about water, waste or local habitats. Match signs to practical actions and relay one notice to a partner in simple words. Avoid complex climate claims unless a short, verified source supports them.

lessons.title: Rules, responsibilities and advice
lessons.task: Contrast must/mustn't with Unit 3 have to/don't have to and Unit 4 should through familiar school/environment scenarios. Partners explain obligations, prohibitions and advice, then check what each means in action. Clarify the difference between not allowed and not necessary.

lessons.title: Plan a small eco-action
lessons.task: Choose a safe school-based or hypothetical local action from supplied options. Pairs share notice facts, suggest actions, respond to suggestions and assign responsibilities. Retrieve Unit 9 uses/materials when selecting safe equipment and Unit 4/Unit 1 habits for a repeatable plan. Each writes three actions and two reasons.

lessons.title: Our eco-action plan: unit checkpoint
lessons.task: Check five new notices, hear each learner explain obligations/prohibition/advice and observe an individual contribution to a shared plan. Collect each learner's actions and reasons. Score message understanding, modal meanings and communication separately; avoid grading family resources or environmental virtue.

units.title: The Great Discovery Challenge
units.themeFocus: Review, integration and a personally chosen familiar discovery
units.languageFocus: Select at least three useful functions from the course: factual description, comparison, past-event account, purpose, reasons or responsible action; audience questions and clarification.
units.example: This invention helps us measure temperature. It is smaller than the first model. We use it to check how warm something is.
units.outcome: Present a discovery using accurate selected facts, descriptions and simple explanations, and respond to an audience.
units.assessmentTask: Great Discovery Showcase: prepare an individual factfile and 1–2-minute illustrated talk, then answer two simple audience questions.
units.support: Choice of familiar animal/place/object/discovery, two short teacher-curated sources, fact grid, labelled visual, keyword cue card and rehearsal. Record support; do not require memorising a script.
units.extension: Add a source comparison or an unexpected audience question as optional stretch; do not turn the core task into a B1 research presentation.

objectives.statement: Select and check useful information about a chosen discovery from short accessible sources.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can find facts and show where they came from.
objectives.successCriteria: Record 4 accurate facts from 2 short teacher-selected sources, identify each source, and label a guess or unknown rather than presenting it as a fact.

objectives.statement: Prepare an illustrated discovery factfile combining familiar language functions.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can make a clear discovery factfile.
objectives.successCriteria: Create 8–10 short linked sentences and a labelled visual; include 4 supported facts and at least 3 useful functions such as description, comparison, past event, purpose or reason.

objectives.statement: Present and explain a discovery to a familiar audience and respond to simple questions.
objectives.learnerStatement: I can present my discovery and answer questions.
objectives.successCriteria: Give a prepared 1–2-minute talk using visuals/keywords, convey 4 facts and one simple explanation, and answer 2 straightforward questions; record repetition and formulation support.

lessons.title: Choose a discovery and gather facts
lessons.task: Choose a familiar discovery topic and read/listen to two short teacher-curated sources. Complete a four-fact grid with source labels and mark any unknowns. Begin with brief retrieval stations for greetings/routines, comparisons/superlatives and a past-event timeline from earlier units; include our/their and ours/theirs when comparing school fact cards. Do not require every reviewed structure in the final talk.

lessons.title: Build an illustrated discovery factfile
lessons.task: Turn the fact grid into an 8–10-sentence factfile and labelled visual, selecting three useful language functions that fit the topic. Start with short retrieval cards for responsibilities/advice, prices/quantities, room/place prepositions, because reasons and a community route. Give feedback on source accuracy, linking and understandable explanations; keep arithmetic separate from language.

lessons.title: Rehearse, ask and improve
lessons.task: Start with a brief retrieval sort on object uses/materials, narrative links and must/mustn't meanings. Learners rehearse a 1–2-minute talk from keywords and visuals, then partners ask two simple questions, request clarification if needed and give one specific improvement suggestion. Revise the talk rather than memorising a full script.

lessons.title: The Great Discovery Showcase and reflection
lessons.task: Check one short new source detail, collect the individual factfile and visual, then hear each learner's prepared discovery talk and two question responses. Score reception, written organisation and oral communication separately using the unit criteria. Record support and select one learning strength plus one next step; do not award an overall CEFR level from this task alone.

grammarTargets.label: Present simple: familiar habits and routines
Comparatives and than in familiar comparisons
Our/their and ours/theirs with clear referents
Have to / don't have to: necessity
Because: a simple reason or explanation
Superlatives with a clear comparison group
Past simple: regular/irregular verbs and did questions
Prices, quantities and polite shopping requests
Ordered directions using imperatives and landmarks
Materials and we use ... to ... for purpose
Narrative links: first, then, suddenly, finally

assessmentNotes: All task counts, timings and response lengths are local WKE planning benchmarks, not official CEFR cut-scores or mandated word counts.
Record a profile by skill and objective: reception, spoken interaction, spoken production and writing. A quiz score does not prove independent speaking.
Separate supported practice from the checkpoint. At checkpoints, allow the repetition, visual cues or formulation support appropriate to the task, and record what was used.

Use a simple local rubric: 0 no interpretable evidence; 1 partial response with frequent modelling; 2 task achieved with appropriate recorded support; 3 task achieved with less support and clear relevant detail. These are teaching judgements, not CEFR certification scores.
Assess communicative success and intelligibility alongside target-language meaning. Minor grammar or accent differences do not automatically invalidate successful A2-oriented communication.
Recheck weak objectives on a different but familiar task after feedback and a delay. Use the later-unit retrieval plan rather than massed revision only at the end.
Resources remain to be selected/created in Libraries; no unverified media, vocabulary packs or activity links are invented by this mapping pass.
pacingSummary: Unit 1: 9 core × 45 minutes, two conditional 25-minute workshops, one optional 30-minute extension. Units 2–12 remain four-slot provisional sketches. The live map has 56 total slots including conditional/optional lessons.
